The Mechanism: When glutamate floods in, it jams open the NMDA receptors, the doors glutamate opens on a brain cell, like a key stuck in the "On" position, and calcium pours in through them. Calcium that high kills the cell only in extremes, a stroke or a brain injury, and that killing is what "excitotoxicity" means (Sattler & Tymianski, 2001), so a storm doesn't mean your neurons are dying. What you feel comes from where the glutamate lands, and under stress it rises in the amygdala, the part that flags threats (Wilson, 2015), so an amygdala firing too hard hands you threat: anxiety, rage, the "itchy brain", and never joy. Block the NMDA receptors there and anxious behaviour drops in animals (Boyle, 2013).

D-serine may help therapy rewrite old memories, since it switches on the spot on the NMDA receptor that this kind of learning runs through (Wolosker, et al, 1999), and it may open the GluD channels as well. The drug actually tested alongside exposure therapy, where you face the feared thing in small safe doses, is a different one, D-cycloserine (DCS), working on that same spot, and across 21 trials with over 1,000 patients it gave the therapy a small push (Mataix-Cols, et al, 2017). It doesn't erase fear, it strengthens whatever you learn in the session, which is why how the session ends matters so much: finish with the fear down and a sense of mastery and DCS helps that stick, and probably D-serine too, but finish overwhelmed and it can cement the fear instead (Smits, et al, 2013).

The Fix ("Lock, Stock, and Barrel"):The Brake (NAC): NAC hands the brain's support cells cystine, an amino acid they swap out for glutamate, and in rats that glutamate sitting outside the synapse trips a brake, the mGluR2/3 receptors, which cut how much glutamate gets fired in (Moran, et al, 2005).

The Lock (Zinc/Magnesium): Magnesium sits in the NMDA channel and plugs it while the cell is resting (Jalali-Yazdi, et al, 2018), and zinc mostly makes the channel open less often, with a weaker plug of its own (Amico-Ruvio, et al, 2011), so less of the voltage gets through either way.

The Signal Dial (GluD Receptors): So if NMDA is the spark, what sets the level? Well, Johns Hopkins researchers recently found that GluD receptors, until now just the things that help build synapses, are channels themselves, and what opens them is D-serine (one of the tools below) and GABA, the chemical that quiets a cell down, not glutamate (Wang, et al, 2025). In people, what turns up is a leak. The mutation behind one inherited ataxia leaves the channel stuck open, and a gene variant that raises the risk of schizophrenia does too (Allen, et al, 2023), so the synapse never gets quiet. My guess is that an armored state jams it the same way, stuck part-way on, so you never come down to a baseline, which from the inside is hyper-vigilance. Nobody has tested that in trauma, so it stays a guess, though the lab already has a drug that shuts these leaking channels.

The Repair (L-Serine): Your brain makes D-Serine out of L-Serine (Wolosker, et al, 1999). So taking L-Serine feeds the spot D-serine switches on, and maybe the GluD channels too, so a session that ends with the fear down and a sense of mastery has a better chance of sticking. The conversion isn't very efficient though, so some people take D-serine itself instead (more risk, but also more benefit).
